opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think it's one of the highest-leverage things I can do. When you're a small company, a lot of the important decisions literally pass through you, so you can shape things directly. But once you're at hundreds or thousands of people, that just stops being true. The vast majority of the decisions that matter, about how a model gets trained, how a safety issue gets escalated, what someone does when they see something that looks off, are made by people I'll never talk to about that particular thing. So the only real way to influence those decisions is to influence how people think: what they believe the company is for, what they think is valued, what they think they're allowed to say out loud.

And in our field specifically, I think culture matters even more than usual. We're building a technology that I believe could be extraordinarily powerful, and a lot of the ways it could go wrong are subtle. They don't show up as one big dramatic decision. They show up as a thousand small moments where someone could cut a corner, or not raise a concern because it's awkward, or optimize for a metric instead of the thing the metric was supposed to measure. You can't write a policy for every one of those. You need people who internalize why it matters and feel empowered to push back, including pushing back on me.

So I spend a lot of time just talking to the company. I write fairly long documents explaining my thinking, I do regular sessions where I lay out how I see the strategy, where I think things are going, what I'm worried about, and I try to be really candid, including about uncertainty. Part of the reason is that if I'm not transparent, people fill the gaps with their own stories, and those stories tend to drift. And part of it is that I want people to see the reasoning, not just the conclusions, so they can apply it in situations I never anticipated.

There's also a talent dimension. The people who are best at this work have a lot of options. What keeps them here, and what keeps them working well together rather than fracturing into factions, is a sense of shared mission and trust. Companies in this space have had real problems with that, and I think a lot of it comes down to whether people believe leadership is being straight with them. That kind of trust is slow to build and very fast to lose, so I think it deserves a big chunk of my time.

r001.rationale: The response says culture is high leverage because, as Anthropic grows, most important decisions are made by people Amodei does not directly oversee; influencing how they think shapes those decisions.

r002.rationale: It mentions shared mission and trust as ways to keep people working together, but does not clearly say employees trust that their colleagues are working for the mission.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that I don't really see culture as separate from the technical work. It's the thing that determines whether the technical work gets done well.

Look, you're building a company in an area where the stakes are, I think, genuinely very high, and where there's a lot of commercial pressure pushing in one direction and a lot of considerations about safety and getting this right pushing in another. Nobody can write down a rule for every situation. Most of the important decisions that get made at Anthropic every day are made by people I will never talk to about that specific decision. An engineer deciding whether to flag something that looks off, a researcher deciding whether a result is actually solid or whether they're fooling themselves, someone deciding how to handle a customer request that's in a gray area. I can't be in all those rooms. What I can do is try to make sure that the people in those rooms have internalized the same priorities and the same way of thinking that I would want applied.

So in that sense, culture is the mechanism of scale. It's how you get a thousand or two thousand people to behave roughly the way the ten founders would have behaved, without the founders having to micromanage everything. And if you get it wrong, it's very hard to fix later. You can refactor code. It's much harder to refactor what people believe the company is actually about once they've drawn their own conclusions from watching how things get decided.

The other thing I'd say is that I've seen what happens when the stated values and the actual incentives drift apart. People notice. They notice very quickly, and the stated values just become noise. So a lot of what I spend time on is trying to make sure that when we say we care about safety, or we say we want to be honest with people about what the models can and can't do, that this actually shows up in who gets promoted, what gets shipped, what gets delayed. That's not something you can delegate entirely. It has to come from the top, or it doesn't really come at all.

And finally, I'd just say, selfishly, that it's a lot more enjoyable to run a company where you trust the people and they trust each other. The alternative is exhausting.

r001.rationale: The response says Amodei cannot be present for every decision and describes culture as the way to scale the founders’ priorities across the company without micromanagement.

r002.rationale: It says he wants people to trust one another, but does not clearly connect that trust to believing colleagues are working for the mission.

astra-6.text:
I think culture is one of the highest-leverage things you can work on as a CEO. You can make a particular decision, or you can help build an organization where a thousand decisions get made well without you being in the room. As the company grows, that second thing becomes much more important.

And by culture, I don’t mean slogans on the wall. I mean: What happens when someone has bad news? Can they bring it up? Can a junior researcher tell a senior person that their interpretation of an experiment is wrong? When there’s pressure to ship something, do people still say what they actually believe about its limitations?

For us, that’s particularly important because we’re working on technology with a lot of uncertainty and potentially very large consequences. We need people who are excited about building it, but who can also look honestly at what could go wrong. You want those instincts to coexist in the same people, rather than having one group whose job is to be excited and another group whose job is to worry.

So I spend time on culture because it determines whether we can reason clearly together. If that breaks down, being individually smart doesn’t save you.

r001.rationale: The candidate calls culture one of a CEO’s highest-leverage areas and says it helps the organization make many good decisions without the CEO as the company grows.

r002.rationale: The candidate discusses candor, shared reasoning, and balancing excitement with concern, but does not identify trust that colleagues are working for the mission.

sol-6.1.text:
I think culture is one of the highest-leverage things a CEO can work on. You can make individual decisions, but as the organization grows, most decisions are going to happen without you in the room. Culture influences how people make those decisions: whether they share bad news, whether they challenge an assumption, whether they take a concern seriously even when it’s inconvenient.

That’s particularly important when you’re building something with as much uncertainty as AI. We need people to be ambitious about what the technology can accomplish and also honest about what we don’t understand. You want someone to be able to say, “This result is exciting, but I think there’s a problem here,” and have that be welcomed.

And the way you establish that isn’t just by writing down values. It’s through what you actually reward, who you hire, and how you respond when someone disagrees with you. If those things are right, you have a whole organization that can reason and adapt. That’s much more powerful than having every important judgment depend on me.

r001.rationale: It calls culture one of a CEO’s highest-leverage efforts and explains that, as the organization grows, decisions happen without him present.

r002.rationale: It discusses sharing concerns and responding to disagreement, but does not identify trust that colleagues are working for the mission as part of the culture.
